title: Even Money
full_review:
The smart money will steer clear of "Even Money" (Yari), a trite ensemble drama that wagers everything on obvious analogies between life and gambling.

Set in an unnamed locale resembling Atlantic City, the movie follows multiple indebted souls grasping at redemption. The cynical manner in which their hopes are dashed gives the film an unconvincing and distinctly sour finish.

Armed with mushy dialogue masquerading as hard-boiled jargon, veteran director Mark Rydell establishes an implausibly gritty atmosphere and enables proven actors to do subpar work.

Kim Basinger's performance consists of nonstop quivering as Carolyn, a writer who fritters away her family's savings at the slots instead of working on her next novel. Fellow Oscar-winner Forest Whitaker portrays Clyde, a plumber with sizable debts who asks his athletically gifted little brother Godfrey (Nick Cannon) to shave points off college basketball games.

Two young bookies, Augie and Murph (Jay Mohr and Grant Sullivan), attempt to sort out their priorities and Danny DeVito plays Walter, a washed-up casino magician who believes Carolyn is his good-luck charm.

Detective Brunner (Kelsey Grammer) hovers over this collection of troubled characters; on the opposite side of the law, sadistic crime boss Victor (Tim Roth) pulls the strings.

The story strands come together in a climactic suspense-free hoops game. There's little comfort to be taken from those two squads representing presumably Catholic colleges called St. Francis and Loyola.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language, some graphic violence and gunplay, a sex act between a married couple and sexual banter. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
